newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Security fears mount as Vranitzky visits Albania.
newsitem.headline: Security fears mount as Vranitzky visits Albania.

text.p: European envoy to Albania Franz Vranitzky, who arrived for talks on elections in the country on Sunday to the sound of incidental gunfire on the streets, appealed for calm as the June 29 poll nears.

Officials at the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), in Albania preparing to bring foreign observers to oversee the poll, said they were very worried about security in parts of the country.

"I will not disguise from you that I myself, and all the members of my team, are quite gravely concerned about violence and about unsecure conditions in some parts of Albania," Vranitzky told a news conference after meeting political leaders.

Vranitzky, trying to keep the country's disputed election process on track, said there had been some achievements on the way to the poll but voiced "a very strong appeal" to all in Albania not to build their future on more violence.
Tension has been mounting as election day nears, with explosions across the country and a failed attempt on President Sali Berisha's life last week.
A short burst of gunfire sounded on the streets near OSCE headquarters soon after Vranitzky went in, an event which residents said was not unusual.

One OSCE observer said he had been frustrated and disappointed on a visit to the south last week to find he could not move unaccompanied by Italian troops: "Even in Bosnia we could go where we wanted," he said.
The OSCE has said it will send over 400 observers to watch the vote; over 100 experts are already in place, moving about with support from an Italian-led multinational force of 6,500 soldiers.

But parts of Albania -- especially in the south -- are still controlled by bandits and gangs, after a wave of chaos and unrest was unleashed by outrage at the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes early this year.

Gerard Stoudman, director of the OSCE's democratic and human rights arm which is overseeing the election operation, said the OSCE will only send observers into the mountainous country's most sensitive areas if it feels they will be safe.
"It is one thing to have one or two teams deployed in ... parts of the country on a voluntary basis," said Stoudman.

"It is a different thing to have more than 200 people driving across the country who you have to control and with whom you have to keep in contact, including among them a substantial number of members of parliament."

Simpler practical concerns include finding enough hotel beds in the capital, whose two main international hotels have only about 300 beds between them; and getting observers across mountain tracks and roads in very poor condition.
"We remain at this day with some worries, some very substantial worries," Stoudman said.

On a separate issue, Vranitzky said he believed that Albania's political parties would work out a solution to a fresh dispute, which arose late on Saturday as smaller opposition parties objected to how the vote will be held.

About eight of Albania's over 20 main parties said they would reconsider whether to run in the parliamentary vote. They were protesting at changes made on Saturday to plans for the distribution of some seats.
